summary: Gives guidance for building a proxy that translates HTTP to CoAP, so an HTTP client can reach resources on a CoAP server. It describes mapping requests and responses.

eli5.summary: A translator lets a web browser talk to tiny devices that speak a lighter language.

questions: what is an http to coap proxy
how to map http requests to coap
how are coap response codes mapped to http
subtitle: How a proxy should translate web (HTTP) requests into CoAP messages for tiny networked devices, and the answers back.

tldr.problem: RFC 7252 only sketches how HTTP maps to CoAP, so different HTTP-to-CoAP proxies can behave differently and an HTTP client cannot count on the same results from each.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives guidelines for an HTTP-to-CoAP proxy (HC Proxy): how to pack a CoAP URI inside an HTTP URI, how to map media types to CoAP content-formats, how to map response codes, and how to handle caching, block-wise transfer, multicast and timeouts.
tldr.outcome: A conforming proxy from one vendor can be swapped for another without breaking API semantics. The security section stresses authentication, careful URI handling and caution with multicast.

today: RFC 8075 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2017. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Map HTTP to CoAP
sections.content:
The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP, RFC 7252) is built for constrained devices and networks, but it is also designed to be easy to bridge to HTTP through a cross-protocol proxy. RFC 7252 covers the basic request method and response code mapping and leaves many details for later.

This RFC fills in those details as guidelines for an HC Proxy, a proxy that acts as an HTTP server towards the client and as a CoAP client towards the device. The stated benefit is less variation between implementations: a conforming proxy from vendor A can be replaced by one from vendor B without breaking API semantics.

The mappings cover the base CoAP specification and the block-wise transfer specification (RFC 7959). Other CoAP extensions are expected to describe their own HTTP mappings.
sections.eli5: Two kinds of devices speak different languages, and a go-between passes messages across. This document is the instruction sheet so every go-between does the job the same way.

sections.title: The HTTP-to-CoAP Proxy
sections.content:
An HC Proxy receives an HTTP request, maps it to the equivalent CoAP request and forwards it to the CoAP server. The CoAP response is then mapped back to an HTTP response for the original client. The proxy can be a forward, reverse or interception proxy. A reverse proxy looks like an origin server to the client, which may not know it is talking to a proxy at all.

The RFC's example deployment puts the proxy at the edge of the constrained network, where it acts as an Application Level Gateway that lets through only authorized inbound HTTP requests and their associated outbound CoAP responses.

Three use cases are listed: a legacy building control application that speaks only HTTP, sensor data made available to third parties on the web (with the proxy configured to pass only GET requests), and a smartphone reaching a home sensor over a mutually authenticated https request.
sections.eli5: The proxy stands at the door of a small clubhouse. Visitors ask it questions in their own language, it asks the club members in theirs, and then it tells the visitors what they said.

sections.title: URI Mapping and Discovery
sections.content:
Web browsers and libraries cannot make HTTP requests to URIs with the scheme coap or coaps. So the CoAP URI (the Target CoAP URI) is packed into an HTTP URI (the Hosting HTTP URI) that points at the proxy, and the proxy unpacks it.

There are three kinds of mapping. The null mapping appends nothing: the client sends a plain HTTP URI and the proxy decides the target by its own private algorithm, typically as a reverse proxy. The default mapping appends the Target CoAP URI as is to the HC Proxy URI. It SHOULD be implemented and SHOULD be on by default. A URI mapping template (a Level 2 URI Template, RFC 6570) lets a proxy describe a different layout.

The scheme can be omitted only if client and proxy have agreed a local default. Without that agreement a scheme-less URI MUST NOT be sent, and the proxy MUST answer it with a 4xx error. If the authority is an IPv6 address, the square brackets must be percent-encoded in the Hosting HTTP URI.

The simple template form uses one variable, tu. The enhanced form uses s, hp, p, q and qq, each at most once, and q and qq MUST NOT be used together.

For discovery, a proxy SHOULD publish its location through the CoRE Link Format (RFC 6690). This RFC defines the resource type core.hc and the link attribute hct carrying the template. If no hct is returned, the default template {+tu} MUST be assumed.
sections.eli5: A web browser cannot write a CoAP address, so the address gets tucked inside a web address like a small letter inside a bigger envelope. The proxy opens the envelope and delivers the letter.

sections.title: Media Type and Content Mapping
sections.content:
HTTP names the kind of data with a media type and content coding. CoAP uses a single small integer, the content-format. The proxy translates both ways. Going from HTTP to CoAP is harder, because there are potentially 1000+ IANA-registered media types but only six content-formats were initially defined in RFC 7252.

If a request has a Content-Type and Content-Encoding combination the proxy cannot map, it SHALL answer 415 (Unsupported Media Type). A failure to map Accept headers SHOULD be silently ignored, and the CoAP request sent with no Accept option. An HTTP Accept: */* MUST map to a CoAP request without an Accept option.

If a CoAP response carries a content-format the proxy does not recognize, the proxy SHALL return the new media type application/coap-payload with a numeric parameter cf, for example application/coap-payload;cf=60.

An optional loose mapping generalizes a specific type to a broader one so it can be mapped, using a lookup table compared from top to bottom. Transcoding payloads, for example XML to EXI or JSON to CBOR, is also optional. The RFC warns that it can inflate maliciously crafted input, lose information, or carry malware risk. Rewriting CoRE Link Format payloads should only be done at the implementer's risk. A CoAP diagnostic payload SHOULD be copied into the HTTP body as text/plain;charset=utf-8 and MUST NOT go into the reason phrase.
sections.eli5: One side labels boxes with long names and the other uses short numbers. The proxy keeps a translation list. If a label is not on the list it uses a generic box marked with the number, rather than guessing.

sections.title: Response Code Mapping
sections.content:
Table 2 of the RFC says which HTTP status each CoAP response code SHOULD map to. Most map one to one, for example 2.05 Content to 200 OK, 4.04 Not Found to 404 and 5.03 Service Unavailable to 503.

Several have special handling. A CoAP 2.02 Deleted or 2.04 Changed becomes 200 OK if the server returned a payload, and 204 No Content if not. A 2.03 Valid becomes 304 Not Modified for a conditional request. A 4.01 Unauthorized becomes 403 Forbidden, because HTTP 401 requires a WWW-Authenticate header that CoAP lacks. A 4.05 Method Not Allowed SHOULD normally become 400 Bad Request, with a reason phrase starting with CoAP server returned 4.05, since a 405 would need an Allow list the proxy usually does not know. The HTTP Retry-After value for a 503 comes from the CoAP Max-Age option when present.

The codes 2.31 Continue and 4.08 Request Entity Incomplete are used only in block-wise transfer between proxy and server and never become HTTP responses.
sections.eli5: When the device answers with its own code, the proxy looks up the matching web code on a chart, so the browser can understand whether things went well or badly.

sections.title: Caching, Block-Wise Transfer and Timeouts
sections.content:
An HC Proxy should cache CoAP responses and reply from cache where applicable. If the HTTP client drops the connection, the proxy should still wait for the CoAP response and cache it. To protect the constrained network, it should also limit concurrent pending CoAP requests, and queue or drop extra requests (returning 503 Service Unavailable). The limit should be configurable.

For busy resources the proxy can use CoAP Observe (RFC 7641) to keep its cache fresh instead of ETag validation. With T_R as the mean time between client requests and T_C as the mean time between changes to the resource, an observation reduces message traffic if and only if T_R < 2*T_C.

An HC Proxy SHOULD support block-wise transfers (RFC 7959). It SHOULD retry a payload-carrying PUT or POST with block-wise transfer after a 4.13 response, and when the message is larger than an implementation-specific BLOCKWISE_THRESHOLD.

Multicast support is optional. A proxy that lacks it SHOULD answer 403 (Forbidden) to a request that maps to CoAP multicast. Finally, the proxy MUST define an internal timeout for each pending CoAP request. With confirmable requests it SHOULD be MAX_RTT + MAX_SERVER_RESPONSE_DELAY, and if the delay is unknown, 250 seconds can be used.
sections.eli5: The proxy writes down answers so it does not keep bothering the tiny devices, and it does not wait forever for one that has gone quiet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The proxy sits at the border of a constrained network, so it is an easy single point of failure. Correct request parsing and URI translation are essential to its security. An HC Proxy MUST implement TLS with a Pre-Shared Key and SHOULD implement TLS with client authentication using X.509 certificates. By default it MUST authenticate all incoming requests before forwarding them to the CoAP server, though an administrator MAY disable this.

Multicast is the main hazard. It can be used as a denial-of-service or amplification vector from a single HTTP request, and querying /.well-known/core can reveal a list of a target's devices. The RFC recommends default-deny access control and strong authentication for multicast resources.

For secured exchanges, rules for translating security contexts (for example https to coaps) should be configurable. By default, accessing a coaps URI is only recommended from a corresponding https URI, and the proxy SHOULD reject a coaps request when no security policy mapping is configured. For URI mapping, the RFC advises denying multicast targets and /.well-known/core by default and whitelisting what may be seen, and offers an HTTPS-only interface to keep the target URI opaque to a passive attacker.
sections.eli5: The proxy is a guard at the door. It checks who is knocking, keeps the list of who lives inside private, and will not shout into the whole building because one visitor asked.

messages.label: HTTP Request
messages.note: Sent to the proxy, which acts as an HTTP server.

messages.label: CoAP Req
messages.note: The proxy maps the request to CoAP and forwards it.

messages.label: HTTP Response
messages.note: The CoAP response is mapped back to HTTP.

data.code:
HC Proxy URI:     https://p.example.com/hc/
Target CoAP URI:  coap://s.example.com/light
Hosting HTTP URI: https://p.example.com/hc/coap://s.example.com/light

viz.caption: SELECTED COAP TO HTTP MAPPINGS (RFC 8075, TABLE 2)

items.label: Deleted
items.desc: Maps to 200 OK if a payload is returned, otherwise 204 No Content.

items.label: Valid
items.desc: Maps to 304 Not Modified for a conditional request.

items.label: Unauthorized
items.desc: Maps to 403 Forbidden, since CoAP has no WWW-Authenticate.

items.label: Method Not Allowed
items.desc: Normally maps to 400 Bad Request; 405 only if the allowed methods are known.

items.label: Request Entity Too Large
items.desc: Maps to 413 Payload Too Large, after block-wise retry has failed.
